speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on achieving our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and stable prices for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: While the unemployment rate remains low, it has edged up, job gains have slowed, and downside risks to employment have risen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, inflation has risen recently and remains somewhat elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In support of our goals, and in light of the shift in the balance of risks, today the Federal Open Market Committee decided to lower our policy interest rate by ¼ percentage point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We also decided to continue to reduce our securities holdings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll have more to say about monetary policy after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Recent indicators suggest that growth of economic activity has moderated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: GDP rose at a pace of around 1½ percent in the first half of the year, down from 2.5 percent last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The moderation in growth largely reflects a slowdown in consumer spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In contrast, business investment in equipment and intangibles has picked up from last year’s pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Activity in the housing sector remains weak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our Summary of Economic Projections, the median participant projects GDP to rise 1.6 percent this year and 1.8 percent next year, a touch stronger than projected in June.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the labor market, the unemployment rate edged up to 4.3 percent in August but remains little changed over the past year at a relatively low level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Payroll job gains have slowed significantly to a pace of just 29,000 per month over the past three months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A good part of the slowing likely reflects a decline in the growth of the labor force due to lower immigration and lower labor force participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Even so, labor demand has softened, and the recent pace of job creation appears to be running below the “breakeven” rate needed to hold the unemployment rate constant.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In addition, wage growth has continued to moderate, while still outpacing inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Overall, the marked slowing in both the supply of and demand for workers is unusual.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In this less dynamic and somewhat softer labor market, the downside risks to employment appear to have risen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our SEP, the median projection for the unemployment rate is 4.5 percent at the end of this year and edges down thereafter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased significantly from its highs in mid-2022 but remains somewhat elevated relative to our 2 percent longer-run goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Estimates based on the consumer price index and other data indicate that total PCE prices rose 2.7 percent over the 12 months ending in August and that, excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 2.9 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These readings are higher than earlier in the year, as inflation for goods has picked up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In contrast, disinflation appears to be continuing for services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Near-term measures of inflation expectations have moved up, on balance, over the course of this year on news about tariffs, as reflected in both market- and survey-based measures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Beyond the next year or so, however, most measures of longer-term expectations remain consistent with our 2 percent inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median projection in the SEP for total PCE inflation is 3.0 percent this year and falls to 2.6 percent in 2026 and to 2.1 percent in 2027.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our monetary policy actions are guided by our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At today’s meeting, the Committee decided to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by ¼ percentage point to 4 to 4¼ percent and to continue reducing the size of our balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Changes to government policies continue to evolve, and their effects on the economy remain uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Higher tariffs have begun to push up prices in some categories of goods, but their overall effects on economic activity and inflation remain to be seen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A reasonable base case is that the effects on inflation will be relatively short lived—a one-time shift in the price level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it is also possible that the inflationary effects could instead be more persistent, and that is a risk to be assessed and managed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our obligation is to ensure that a one-time increase in the price level does not become an ongoing inflation problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the near term, risks to inflation are tilted to the upside and risks to employment to the downside—a challenging situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: When our goals are in tension like this, our framework calls for us to balance both sides of our dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: With downside risks to employment having increased, the balance of risks has shifted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Accordingly, we judged it appropriate at this meeting to take another step toward a more neutral policy stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: With today’s decision, we remain well positioned to respond in a timely way to potential economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will continue to determine the appropriate stance of monetary policy based on the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our SEP, FOMC participants wrote down their individual assessments of an appropriate path for the federal funds rate, based on what each participant judges to be the most likely scenario for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median participant projects that the appropriate level of the federal funds rate will be 3.6 percent at the end of this year, 3.4 percent at the end of 2026, and 3.1 percent at the end of 2027.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This path is ¼ percentage point lower than projected in June.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As is always the case, these individual forecasts are subject to uncertainty, and they are not a Committee plan or decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Policy is not on a preset course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Fed has been assigned two goals for monetary policy—maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to supporting maximum employment, bringing inflation sustainably to our 2 percent goal, and keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our success in delivering on these goals matters to all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand that our actions affect communities, families, and businesses across the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everything we do is in service to our public mission, and we at the Fed will do everything we can to achieve our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I look forward to our discussion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we did welcome a new Committee member today, as we always do, and the Committee remains united in pursuing our dual-mandate goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re strongly committed to maintaining our independence, and beyond that I really don’t have anything to share.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s certainly possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’re beginning to see—we have begun to see [increased] goods prices showing through into higher inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, actually, the increase in goods prices accounts for most of the increase in inflation or, perhaps, all of the increase in inflation over the course of this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Those are not very large effects at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we do expect them to continue to build over the course of the rest of the year and into next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s also possible that there may be effects on employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I would say, if you’re looking at why employment is doing what it’s doing, that’s much more about the change in immigration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the supply of workers has, obviously, come way down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s very little growth, if any, in the supply of workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And at the same time, demand for workers has also come down quite sharply and to the point where we see what I’ve called a “curious balance.” Typically, when we say things are “in balance,” that sounds good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, in this case, the balance is because both supply and demand have come down quite sharply, now demand coming down a little more sharply because we see—we now see the unemployment rate edging up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I don’t think we can say that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What we can say is this: that over the course of this year, we’ve kept our policy at a restrictive level—and people have different views, but a clearly restrictive level, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we were able to do that over the course of this year because the labor market was in very solid condition, with strong job creation and all those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think if you go back to April and now look at the revised job-creation numbers for May, June, July, and August, you can kind of—I can no longer say that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So what that means is that the risks, which—the risks were clearly tilted toward inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would say they’re moving toward equality.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Maybe they’re not quite at equality—we don’t need to know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we do know that they’ve moved meaningfully toward greater equality—the risks between the two goals—and that suggests that we should be moving in the direction of neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s what we did today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There wasn’t widespread support at all for a 50 basis point cut today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I think we’ve done—we’ve done very large rate hikes and very large rate cuts in the last five years, and you tend to do those at a time when you feel that policy is out of place and needs to move quickly to a new place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s not at all what I feel, certainly now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I feel like our policy has been doing the right thing so far this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we were right to wait and see how tariffs and inflation and the labor market evolved.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we’re now reacting to the much lower level of job creation and other evidence of softening in the labor market and saying, well, those risks are maybe not fully balanced but moving in the direction of balance now, and so that warrants a change in policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, I think you could think of this, in a way, as a risk-management cut, because if you look at the SEP, actually the projections for growth this year and next actually ticked up just a little bit and inflation and unemployment didn’t really move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What’s different now is that you see a very different picture of the risks to the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’ve seen—you know, we were looking at 150,000 jobs a month at the time of the last meeting, and now we see the revisions and we see the new numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I didn’t—I don’t want to put too much emphasis on payroll job creation, but it’s just one of the things that suggests that the labor market is really cooling off.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that tells you that it’s time to take that into account in our, you know, in our policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, so I would look at it this way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We fully understand and appreciate that we need to remain fully committed to restoring 2 percent inflation on a sustained basis, and we will do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, we’ve got to weigh the risks to the two goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I would say since—really, since April, to me the risks of higher and more persistent inflation have probably become a little less.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s partly because the labor market has softened, GDP growth has slowed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so I would just say that the risks there have been less than one might think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And in terms of the labor market, what we’re seeing is, unemployment is still low—it’s still at a relatively low rate, but we’re seeing downside risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, I was—I was saying that what’s happening in the labor market has more to do with immigration than it has to do with tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That was the question I was answering.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I wouldn’t say that all of what’s happening in the labor market is due to tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, you clearly have a slowing due to immigration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You clearly have a slowing in demand, which is now perhaps more than that in supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we know that because the unemployment rate has ticked up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s how—that’s what I meant by that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, I mean, you’re right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It does say we’re going to get to 2 percent inflation in 2028—at the end of ’28.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s—you know, that’s literally how you put the projections together.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re writing down a rate path which is designed to create, over the course of the SEP, you know, time frame, 2 percent inflation, and maximum employment too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s, that’s all that is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we don’t—no one really knows where the economy will be in three years, but the nature of the exercise is to write down policy that you believe would return to the 2 percent goal over the—at least by the end of the exercise.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So our expectation, and you can see this consistently through the year, has been that inflation will move up this year, but that the—basically, because of the effects on goods prices from tariffs—but that those will turn out to be a one-time price increase, as opposed to creating an inflationary process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s been our forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Pretty much every—all the individual forecasts say that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have to—our job is literally to make sure that that is what happens.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we will do that job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Right now, the situation we’re in is that we see inflation—we continue to expect it to move up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Maybe not as high as we would have expected it to move up a few months ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The pass-through into—of the tariffs into inflation has been slower and smaller.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market has softened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the case for there being a persistent inflation outbreak is less.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so that’s why we think it’s time for us really to acknowledge that the risks to the other mandate have grown, and that we should move in the direction of neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll do what we need to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we have two mandates, and we try to balance them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: For a long time, our framework says that when our two goals are in tension—this is quite an unusual situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Because our tools can’t do two things at once.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So and then that’s—we think about those things, and we see—as I mentioned, we have been—our policy had been really skewed toward inflation for a long time, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now we see that there’s downside risk clearly in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we’re moving in a direction of more neutral policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s an interesting labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And obviously we think it’s appropriate that we reduce our rates so that we become more neutral, which will be—which, presumably, will be better for the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You see people who are sort of more at the margins—so kids coming out of college and younger people, minorities—are having a hard time finding jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The overall job-finding rate is very, very low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: However, the layoff rate is also very low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’ve got a low—a low-firing, low-hiring environment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the concern is that if you start to see layoffs, the people who are laid off won’t—there won’t be a lot of hiring going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that could very quickly flow into higher unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In a healthier economy, healthier labor market, there would be jobs for those people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But now the hiring rate is very, very low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s been a growing concern over the last few months, and it’s one of the reasons why we think it’s appropriate that we begin to shift our policy focus toward a more balanced one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think we are—we’re in a meeting-by-meeting situation, and we’re going to be looking at the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, let me say a word about the SEP, really, here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we often point this out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What the SEP is, it’s an accumulation—a cumulation of the individual projections of 19 people showing what they believe at a particular moment in time to be the most likely path for the economy and, thus, the appropriate path for monetary policy as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And as you know, we don’t—we don’t debate or try to agree on what that is; we just write them down and cumulate them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We do sometimes discuss them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we always say we’re not on a preset path, and we really mean that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The actual decisions we make are going to be based on the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks at the time the decisions are actually made.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you will have seen that we have 10 participants out of 19 who wrote down two or more cuts for the remainder of the year, and 9 who wrote down fewer than—in fact, in a good number of cases no more cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So rather than looking at—so rather than looking at this as certainty, I would encourage people, as always, to look at the SEP as—through the lens of probability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so there are—there are different possible outcomes and likelihoods rather than “this one is certain, and this one isn’t happening.” So that’s what I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it is such an unusual situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Ordinarily, when the labor market is weak, inflation is low; and when the labor market is really strong, that’s when you’ve got to be careful about inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we have a situation where we have two-sided risk, and that means there’s no risk-free path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so it’s quite a difficult situation for policymakers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s not at all surprising to me that you have a range of views.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not so much about having different views for the path of the economy, but—it’s partly that, but it’s also partly about what’s the right thing to do in light of this—of the tension between the two goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so it’s natural.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think it would actually be surprising if you didn’t have a pretty wide range of views based, you know, in this kind of highly unusual situation, and we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, we get together, we discuss—we have a great discussion, and then we decide what to do and we act.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But you’re right that it is—it’s a wide dispersion of views, and I think that’s understandable and natural in the current situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Look, it’s deeply in our culture to do—to do our work based on the incoming data and never consider anything else.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s just—everybody here who’s at the Fed really feels strongly about that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, you’ll know it by the way we talk about what we’re doing, by the speeches that people give, by the decisions that we make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’ll know that we’re just still going to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s all we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we don’t—we don’t frame these questions at all or see them in terms of political outcomes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, that’s the framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think people find it hard to believe that that’s just—that is not at all the way we think about things at the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re taking a longer perspective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re trying to, you know, serve the American people as best we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think—I think you would be able to tell.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t—I don’t believe we’ll ever get to that place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I would say we’re doing our work exactly as we always have now, and people are—they’re making their arguments, and we’re having, really, a great discussion around these challenging issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So— VICTORIA GUIDA.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I see it as a court case that it would be inappropriate for me to comment on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, on the QCEW, the revision that we saw was almost exactly what we expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It was amazing how close the expectation was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the reason for that is for the last bunch of quarters, there’s been a—almost a predictable overcount.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think the, you know, the Bureau of Labor Statistics really does understand this, and they’re working hard to fix it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s got to do—of course, it has something to do with low response rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s also got to do with what’s called the birth–death model, because a good amount of job creation happens around new companies, and how many go out of business, how many are founded.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s just really hard.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You can’t survey for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’ve got to have a model that predicts that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s quite difficult to do, especially when the economy is undergoing big changes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And they’ve been working on that and are making progress on it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, the data we get is still well good enough for us to do our work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: To the extent we have issues around data right now, it’s about low response rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s happened all over—all over, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Response rates are just lower to surveys now, both in and out of the government.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s no great secret.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we want higher response rates, and we need those to have, you know, less volatile data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the way to get that is to make sure that the agencies that collect the data have sufficient resources to drive higher response rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not a complicated problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s what it takes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not a mystery.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what it takes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The other thing I’ll say, Edward, is in the case of the job creation, the first—the response rate is quite low for the first month, or lower for the first month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: By the time you get to the second or third month, you’re still collecting responses for that last month—for that prior month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you get to the place where the data are much more reliable by the second, and certainly the third, month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s not that we don’t get the data—it’s just that we get it a little later.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we have to live life looking through the windshield rather than the rearview mirror, as you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And all I can tell you is we see where we are now, and we take appropriate action.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we took that appropriate action today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, I hadn’t say that I thought a ¼ point would make a huge difference to the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the market has already—has already been baking in expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think our policy path really does matter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think it’s important that we use our tools to support the labor market when we do see signs like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I did mention that, you know, you see minority unemployment going up, you see younger people—people who are more vulnerable economically, more susceptible to economic cycles.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s one of the reasons, in addition to just overall lower payroll job creation, that shows you that at the margin the labor market is weakening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would also point to labor force participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Some part of the significant decline in labor force participation over the last year has probably been cyclical in nature, rather than just the usual aging process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we put all those together, and we see that the labor market is softening, and we don’t need it to soften any more, don’t want it to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we use our tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, it starts with a 25 basis point rate cut, but we—you know, the market’s also pricing in a rate path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m not blessing what the market’s doing at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m just saying it’s not just one action.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t say that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, you’re right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Those are two—we’re getting unusually large amounts of economic activity through the AI build-out and corporate investment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know how long that will go on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No one does.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of spending, you saw the consumer spending numbers were well above expectations, and that may well be skewed toward higher-earning consumers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s a lot of anecdotal evidence to suggest that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nonetheless, it’s spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, I mean, I think the economy is—you know, it’s moving along.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Economic growth is going to be 1½ percent or better this year, maybe a little better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Forecasts have been coming up, as you can see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So labor market is—unemployment is low, but—you know, downside risks—but it’s still a low unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s how we see it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I—of course, I’m not going to comment on anything the secretary says or, really, any other officer says.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So in terms of reform at the Fed, you know, we just—we just went through a lengthy and I think very successful process of updating our monetary policy framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would say there’s a lot of work going on behind the scenes around the assets we have in the Federal Reserve System and at the Board.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re actually going through a 10 percent head count reduction through the whole Fed, including the Board and all the Reserve Banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Employment at the Fed at the end of that will be basically at the same level it was more than 10 years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we will have had zero job growth for more than a decade when we’re finished with that, and I think we’ll probably do more than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think we’re certainly open to constructive criticism and ways to do our jobs better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re certainly open to, you know, to always trying to do better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there’s great uncertainty around that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think my view—which is also a bit of a guess, but widely shared I think—is that you are seeing some effects, but it’s not the main thing driving it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so a particular focus on young people coming out of college and, yeah, there may be something there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It may be that companies or other institutions that have been hiring younger people right out of college are able to use AI more than they had in the past.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That may be part of the story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s also part of the story, though, that, you know, job creation more broadly has slowed down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economy has slowed down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so it’s probably a number of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, yeah, it’s probably a factor.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Hard to say how big it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, if you—you can take goods—just sort of the broad goods category, and last year goods inflation was negative.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you go back 25 years, that was the typical thing was that goods inflation was—goods prices generally went down, even adjusting for quality.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that was not the case during the pandemic, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Goods inflation went very high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we had essentially returned to zero or slightly negative inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, I think goods inflation over the course of the past year is 1.2 percent, which doesn’t sound like a lot, but it’s a big change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we think—I mean, analysts have different views, but we think it’s contributing, you know, 0.3 or 0.4, something like that, to the current core PCE inflation reading, which is 2.9 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s contributing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What seems to be happening is that, you know, the tariffs are not—mostly not being paid by exporters, mostly being paid by, really, the companies that sit between the exporter and the consumer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if you buy something and you sell it through retail or you use it to make a product, you’re probably taking a lot of those costs on and not able to pass it fully along to the consumer yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That appears to be what we’re seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: All of those companies and entities in the middle, they’ll tell you that they have every intention of passing that through in time, but they’re not doing that now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: To the consumer, the pass-through has been pretty small.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s been slower and later—slower and smaller than we thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the evidence is very clear that there’s some pass-through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I have nothing new on that for you today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there’s 12 voters—19 participants, of whom 12 vote, as you know, on a rotating basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So no one voter, you know, can really—the only way for any voter to really move things around is to be incredibly persuasive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the only way to do that, in the context in which we work, is to make really strong arguments based on the data and one’s understanding of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s really all that matters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s how it’s going to work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think that is the way the institution—that’s in the DNA of the institution.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s not going to change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our response is we’re going to do everything we can to use our tools to achieve the goals that Congress has given us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re not going to get distracted by anything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think that’s what we’re going to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re just going to keep doing our jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think there’s quite a wide assessment that the situation has changed with respect to the labor market, whereas we could still say—and did say—in July, at the time of the July meeting, that the labor market was in solid condition, and we could point to 150,000 jobs per month, and many other things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think that the new data that we’ve had—and it’s not just payrolls, it’s other things as well—suggests that there really is meaningful downside risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I said there was downside risk then, but I think that that downside risk is now a reality.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And there’s clearly more downside risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think that was—I think that’s broadly accepted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so that meant different things for different people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, some wrote down—almost everyone wrote down support of this cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And some supported more cuts, and some didn’t, as you will see from the dot plot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s just the way—that’s just the way it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, people have—you have people who take this work very seriously, think about it all the time, do their work, discuss it with our colleagues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we endlessly discuss this between ourselves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then we have a meeting where we put it all out on the table.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And this is what you get.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you’re right, there is a—there’s a range of views in the dots.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think that’s, like I said, very unsurprising given the quite unusual—historically unusual nature of the challenges that we face.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But let’s remember, though, the unemployment rate’s 4.3 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economy is growing at 1½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s not a bad economy, or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve seen much more challenging economic times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But from a policy standpoint, the standpoint of what we’re trying to accomplish, it’s challenging to know what to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There are, as I mentioned earlier, there are no risk-free paths now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not incredibly obvious what to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we have to keep our eye on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, we cannot ignore and must keep our eye on maximum employment, which is—those are our two equal goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you will see that there are just a range of views on what to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nonetheless, we came together today at the meeting and acted with a high degree of unity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, so there are many different ways to calculate it and none of them is perfect, but, you know, it’s clearly come way down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There are—you could say it’s somewhere between zero and 50,000, and you’d be right or wrong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, there’s just many different ways to do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So wherever it was—150,000, 200,000 a few months ago—it’s come down quite significantly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s because a very—a lower amount of people are joining the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor force is really not growing much at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s a lot of where the supply of labor was coming from over the last three—two or three years, so we’re not getting that now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re also—we’ve gotten much lower demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s interesting that supply and demand have really come down together so far, except now we do have inflation—sorry, unemployment ticking up outside, just one tick outside of the range where it’s been for a year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Four point three percent is still a low level, but, you know, I think this level of—this speedy decline in both supply and demand has certainly gotten everyone’s attention.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, that would be great.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’d love that to happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I don’t know that you see a big tension there, but it’s gratifying to see that economic activity is holding and—you know, so it’s a good, a good bit from consumption.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It looks like consumption was stronger than expected—what we got earlier this week, I guess.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And also we’re getting, you know—a fairly narrow sector is producing a lot of economic activity, which is the AI build-out and, you know, business investment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, we watch all of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I would say we—you know, we did move up, the median for growth for this year actually moved up in the SEP between the June and September SEPs, so—and, really, the inflation and labor market didn’t change much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s really the risks that we’re seeing to the labor market that were the focus of today’s decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, housing is an interest-sensitive activity, so it’s at the very center of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: When the pandemic hit and we cut rates to zero, the housing companies were incredibly grateful and it was really—they said that was the only thing that kept them going was that we cut so aggressively and provided credit and things like that, and they were able to finance because we did that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The other side of that is when inflation gets high and we raise rates—and you’re right, it does burden the housing industry.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so rates have come down a bit, and as that happens we don’t set the—we don’t set mortgage rates, but our policy rate changes do tend to affect mortgage rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that has been happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’ll, of course, raise demand, lower borrowing rates for builders, will help, you know, get builders—will help supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so some of that should happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think most analysts think that it would have to be pretty big changes for it to matter a lot for the—big changes in rates to matter a lot for the housing sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, the other thing is by—you know, by achieving maximum employment and price stability, that’s a strong economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s a good economy for housing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then the last thing I’ll say is, you know, there’s a deeper problem here that is not a cyclical problem that the Fed can address, and that just is a pretty much nationwide housing shortage, or a lot of places in the country just don’t have enough housing for people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, all of the areas around metropolitan areas—like Washington, for example—are very built up, and so you’re having to build farther and farther out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that—so that’s where it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, forecasting is very difficult, even in placid times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, as I’ve mentioned before, forecasters are a humble lot, with much to be humble about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think right now is a particularly challenging time, even more uncertain than usual.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so I don’t know any forecaster anywhere really—ask any of the forecasters whether they have great confidence in their forecast right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think they’ll honestly say “no.” JENNIFER SCHONBERGER.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you, Chair Powell.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Jennifer Schonberger with Yahoo Finance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, I think we’re—you know, we’re cutting the size of our balance sheet quite marginally now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As you know, with the balance sheet, we’re still in an abundant-reserves condition.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ve said that we would stop somewhat above a—somewhat above an ample-reserves level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s where we are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re—you know, we’re getting closer to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re monitoring it very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t think that that has, at all, significant macroeconomic effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These are pretty small numbers moving around inside a giant economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, the level of runoff is not very large.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I wouldn’t attribute macroeconomic consequences to that, at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we always think of it as the dual mandate, maximum employment and price stability, for a long time, because we think moderate, long-term interest rates are something that will result from stable inflation—low and stable inflation and maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we don’t—we haven’t thought about that for a very long time as a third mandate that requires independent action.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s where that is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And there’s no thought of—as far as I’m concerned, there’s no thought of considering that, you know, considering that we somehow incorporate that in as something in a different way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, we’re aware of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think default rates have been kind of ticking up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we do watch that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re not at a level—I don’t believe they’re at a level where, overall, they’re, you know, terribly concerning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it is something that we watch.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, lower rates should support economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know that one rate cut will have, you know, a visible effect on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But over time, you know, a strong economy with a strong labor market is what we’re—what we’re aiming for, and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that should help.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And our goals are maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we take the actions that we take with an eye on those goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Separately—and that’s why we did what we did today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Separately, we monitor financial stability very, very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, I would say it’s a mixed picture, but households are in good shape, banks are in good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Overall, households are still in good shape in the aggregate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I know that people at the lower end of the income spectrum are under pressure, obviously.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But from a financial stability perspective, we monitor that picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t have a view that there’s a right or wrong level of asset prices for any particular financial asset, but we monitor the whole picture, really looking for structural vulnerabilities, and I would say those are not elevated right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, as you said, shorter-term inflation expectations have tended to respond to near-term inflation, so if inflation goes up, inflation expectations will predict that it takes just a little while to get back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Fortunately, throughout this period, longer-term inflation expectations, both breakeven in the markets and almost all of the longer-term surveys—Michigan being a bit of an outlier lately—have been just rock solid in terms of, you know, running at levels that are consistent with 2 percent inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we don’t take that for granted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We actually assume that our actions have a real effect on that, and that, you know, we need to, you know, continually show and also mention/discuss our commitment to 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so you’ll hear us doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, we’re—as I mentioned, it’s a difficult situation because we have risks that are both affecting the labor market and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Those are our two goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we have to balance those two.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: When they’re both at risk, we have to balance them, and that’s really what we’re trying to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t— the latter part of your question was about independence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I don’t see market participants—I don’t see that that’s something they’re factoring in right now in terms of setting interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thanks very much.
